crumbs.name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences

reading.body:
Training is where successful AI adoption gets its money's worth, and in the EU it is now a legal duty as well as good practice.

The pattern in the data is that the programmes which invest most in training are the ones described as successful. Moderna's AI Academy, built with Carnegie Mellon and Coursera, trained more than 2,000 employees. That is a workforce-scale commitment, not a pilot, and it is the only company figure the data gives.

For AI specifically, the training content is not generic. It covers how AI works at a practical level, its limits and risks, company policies, and safe use for each role. That matters because the failure mode in regulated industries is not a model that cannot do the task, it is a person who does not know where the model stops being reliable or what the internal rules permit.

The EU AI Act requires providers and deployers to ensure staff have sufficient AI literacy, and that obligation became applicable on 2 February 2025. Training records are therefore worth keeping, since they serve as evidence of meeting the duty. The data does not say how many companies comply, what enforcement looks like, or whether training changes adoption outcomes. It covers one named programme and one legal requirement, and nothing about cost, completion rates, or effect on AI deployment.

The training obligation attaches to the role, not the person. The data describes four distinct audiences, general literacy for all staff, practical skills tied to everyday tasks, deeper technical training for builders, and governance training for managers who approve uses. A single curriculum cannot serve all four, so the compliance question is not whether staff were trained but whether each role received the content its decisions require.

The EU duty and the adoption benefit pull in the same direction but are not the same thing. The AI Act requires sufficient AI literacy among staff using AI, and the data says training records double as evidence of meeting that duty. That makes documentation part of the deliverable, not an administrative afterthought. A programme that teaches well but records nothing satisfies the adoption goal and fails the legal one.

Moderna's number is the only scale figure in the data, and it is a headcount rather than an outcome. More than 2,000 employees trained says nothing about whether those employees used AI differently afterward. The data does not connect the training to any deployment, productivity, or quality result, so the Moderna case establishes that workforce-scale programmes exist, not that they work.

What does AI literacy training actually cover?
It covers how AI works at a practical level, its limits and risks, company policies, and safe use for each role. The content is role-specific rather than one general course for everyone.

Should training records be kept?
Yes, especially in the EU, as evidence of meeting the AI literacy duty. The data treats the record as the proof of compliance, so the record has to exist alongside the training.

When did the EU AI Act's AI literacy obligation take effect?
It became applicable on 2 February 2025. The data gives that date and no enforcement or penalty detail.

How many employees did Moderna's AI Academy train?
More than 2,000, according to Coursera's case study. Moderna built the academy with Carnegie Mellon and Coursera, and it is the only company training figure in the data.

Does the data show that training improves AI adoption outcomes?
No. The data states that training is consistently identified as a deciding factor and that successful programmes invest in it most, but it holds no measurement of adoption, productivity, or quality change attributable to training.

How many companies comply with the AI literacy requirement?
The data does not say. It also does not describe what enforcement looks like, what training costs, or what completion rates look like.

sections.heading: What it means for a life sciences leader

siblings.name: Governing AI in a Regulated Company

explainer:
Training is consistently identified as a deciding factor in whether AI programmes deliver. Effective programmes teach different things to different roles: general literacy for all staff, practical skills tied to everyday tasks, deeper technical training for builders, and governance training for managers who approve uses.

In the EU, training now also serves compliance, since the AI Act requires AI literacy among staff using AI. Recording who completed which training, and tying content to the tools and policies actually in use, satisfies that duty while improving results.

What people actually need to learn

Most AI training in life sciences companies has taught people how to prompt a chatbot. That is the smallest part of the skill. What regulated work needs is judgement about when a model's output can be trusted, how to verify it, what data may be entered into which tool, and when a task is out of bounds. A medical writer needs to know that a citation must be checked. A quality engineer needs to know that a model is a change to a validated process. A sales representative needs to know that generated text is promotional speech.

Three layers of training that work

First, a short foundation for everyone: what the tools can and cannot do, the company's rules on data and approved tools, and how to report a problem. Second, role specific training built around the actual tasks of each function, with examples of good and bad output from that function's own work. Third, deeper skills for the people who build, validate or govern AI: data provenance, validation approaches, model monitoring and the relevant regulatory guidance. The second layer is the one most companies skip and the one that changes behaviour.

Measuring whether it worked

Completion rates say nothing. Better measures are whether verification steps are actually followed, whether the number of policy breaches falls, whether approved tools displace unapproved ones, and whether people in each function can describe the specific failure modes of the tools they use. Companies that track those see training as a control, which in a regulated industry is what it is.
